summary.text: 来 is a graphic variant of 來, traditionally interpreted as a picture of wheat. Its familiar meaning is “come” or “arrive.” A common proposal is that the wheat sign was reused for a similar-sounding word, though the plant’s original spoken name is not established.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph is traditionally read as a wheat plant, with a stem, paired leaves, and an ear-like top. The upper mark may instead be a distinguishing or ornamental stroke, so its exact botanical reference is uncertain.

history.text: The traditional graph 來 is recorded in oracle-bone and bronze materials, as well as later manuscript and script forms. This long record does not establish an exact sequence of stroke changes or when the wheat and “come” uses diverged.
来 is a graphic variant of 來 associated with clerical writing and graphic deformation.

uncertainties.text: A common explanation is that the wheat graph was reused to write a different word because the words sounded similar. Reconstructions show related sound forms for 來’s wheat and “come” uses, but do not establish the plant’s original spoken name or prove why the graph was reused. A traditional account instead links “come” with wheat said to have arrived from Heaven; the origin and chronology remain unresolved.

The earliest securely dated use of either meaning is unresolved. The transmitted Odes phrase 貽我來牟 refers to grain but does not show that 來 alone meant wheat or establish the poem’s date; reported oracle-bone contexts also do not settle which use came first.
The upper strokes have been read as part of the wheat ear, a distinguishing mark, or ornament. Their precise botanical meaning and the graphic transitions between early forms remain uncertain.

senses.text: The graph is traditionally explained as a picture of wheat, and lexicographic and transmitted literary evidence records it in grain terminology. The earliest securely dated use of 來 alone for wheat is unresolved.

limitations.text: The proposed original wheat meaning and the sound-based explanation of “come” are not conclusively resolved against the traditional account linking arrival and wheat semantically. The earliest wheat use and the point when the meanings separated are not securely dated.
The recorded senses do not establish specific links among “come,” “return,” future or past uses, and grammatical functions; no semantic developments are asserted.

The surviving evidence reports early forms of 來 but does not provide an inspectable candidate image with verified reuse rights. The plant-like reading and the interpretation of the upper stroke remain debated, and the evidence does not establish when the wheat and ‘come’ uses separated.
